strengths: RALU addresses an important practical problem—training-free spatial acceleration of diffusion transformers—with an intuitive three-stage design that concentrates computation around edge regions while retaining low-resolution processing elsewhere.

The empirical gains are substantial on two strong flow-matching models. At comparable compute, RALU consistently improves over Bottleneck Sampling and temporal baselines; for example, at roughly 7× FLUX acceleration it obtains FID 28.68 versus 38.16 for Bottleneck Sampling, while also improving NIQE and CLIP-IQA.

The evaluation covers latency, FLOPs, several image-quality and text-alignment metrics, qualitative comparisons, two acceleration regimes per model, and uncurated FLUX samples. Reporting measured A100 latency in addition to theoretical FLOPs is valuable.

The correlated-noise formulation provides a useful motivation for resolution-transition artifacts, and the paper explicitly derives the covariance constraint and reports the optimized stage schedules and noise parameters.
Demonstrating compatibility with caching is practically useful: adding caching raises the reported FLUX speedups from 4.13× to 5.00× and from 7.02× to 7.94× with relatively modest metric changes.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and its diagrams clearly communicate the main pipeline and the distinction between aliasing and noise-timestep mismatch artifacts.
weaknesses: Material: the central components are not isolated convincingly. NT-DM is evaluated mainly by perturbing its selected parameters by ±20%, without a quantitative comparison against no rescheduling, noise injection alone, heuristic rescheduling, or direct distribution matching alternatives. Likewise, edge-based selection is not compared quantitatively with random, uniform, saliency-based, or full early upsampling at matched FLOPs. The limited examples in Figures 4 and 6 do not establish that the proposed mechanisms cause the aggregate gains.

Material: the mathematical presentation is internally inconsistent. Appendix Eq. (S2) gives the target covariance as (1−s)^2Σ, whereas Eq. (S4) uses (1−s)^2I; the subsequent cancellation argument and solution require the latter. More broadly, the covariance derivation assumes regular 2× nearest-neighbor upsampling, but the actual Stage 2 representation mixes high- and low-resolution regions. The manuscript does not derive or justify why the same covariance and rescheduling construction applies at irregular region boundaries.

Material: evaluation uncertainty is not reported. There are no repeated-seed statistics, confidence intervals, or human preference study, even though several metric differences are small and the claimed benefit concerns visually localized artifacts that FID, NIQE, and CLIP-IQA may not reliably capture.

Material: the FID protocol is underspecified—the real-image reference set, generated sample count, prompt source, preprocessing, and feature implementation are not stated. This makes the reported FID improvements difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The claim of “minimal degradation” is somewhat overstated relative to the full models. For example, SD3 at 3× falls from 0.673 to 0.597 on GenEval, and FLUX at 7× falls from 0.707 to 0.681 on CLIP-IQA. RALU is clearly favorable to compute-matched baselines, but preservation relative to the unaccelerated model is metric-dependent.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of algorithmic pseudocode or sufficient implementation detail for the mixed-resolution DiT input: construction and merging of heterogeneous-resolution tokens, positional coordinates, boundary handling, exact top-k patch definition, Canny settings, and several sampling details are unclear.

Presentation refinements include the incorrect downward arrow for GenEval in Table 4, several grammatical issues, and an incorrect citation association for Stable Diffusion 3. These are readily fixable but add ambiguity to an already technical method.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: training-free spatial acceleration of diffusion transformers. Mixed-resolution processing is complementary to temporal caching and can reduce token-processing cost substantially.

RALU combines low-resolution denoising, selective early upsampling of edge-heavy regions, and full-resolution refinement in a conceptually intuitive framework. The correlated-noise derivation provides a reasonable basis for handling resolution transitions in rectified-flow models.

The evaluation covers two substantial text-to-image models, FLUX.1-dev and Stable Diffusion 3, with latency and FLOPs reported on an A100. At comparable compute, RALU generally improves image-quality metrics over Bottleneck Sampling and the evaluated temporal baselines.

The paper includes baseline configurations, stage schedules, caching experiments, extensive qualitative examples, and uncurated RALU samples. The reported 4–7x FLUX and 2–3x SD3 operating points could be practically useful.
weaknesses: The central design claims are inadequately ablated. There is no quantitative comparison of edge-based selection against random, uniform, attention-based, or other region selection; no complete component ablation separating early upsampling, correlated noise, and timestep matching; and no quantitative assessment of aliasing. Figures 4 and S1 provide only isolated qualitative examples, so they do not establish that edges are generally the right regions or that both proposed components cause the reported gains.

The NT-DM evidence is particularly weak. Table 4 merely rescales the selected parameters and omits a no-NT-DM baseline. The nominal parameters are best only on NIQE, tie another setting on CLIP-IQA, and are worse than 0.8×{h_k} on GenEval (0.632 versus 0.654). Thus, the stated conclusion that JSD-minimizing parameters perform better overall is not supported consistently by the table. GenEval is also incorrectly marked with a downward arrow there.

Important implementation details needed to reproduce the central mixed-resolution operation are absent: how irregular low- and high-resolution tokens are ordered and assigned positional coordinates, how boundaries and overlaps are handled, the exact clean-latent/Tweedie computation, Canny settings, patch construction, and the Stage-2 upsampling ratio used for the main results. The numerical-search domain and procedure for NT-DM are likewise unspecified.

The mathematical presentation contains an internal inconsistency. Appendix Eq. S2 labels the next state as an upsampled latent and states covariance proportional to Sigma in the prose/display, whereas Eq. S4 performs matching to an identity-covariance high-resolution flow state. The intended target appears recoverable, but the notation as written does not provide a fully consistent derivation.

Evaluation reporting is incomplete. The paper does not specify the reference dataset, generated sample count, or protocol used for FID, NIQE, and CLIP-IQA; nor does it report repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, batch size, precision, warm-up policy, or timing repetitions. These omissions make differences such as FID 28.30 versus 28.42 or GenEval 0.639 versus 0.634 difficult to interpret.

There is no human preference or artifact-focused evaluation. This matters because the main claimed advantage is suppression of visible aliasing and mismatch artifacts, while the automatic metrics are generic and sometimes disagree. Qualitative comparisons use outputs with substantially different content and include uncurated samples only for RALU, limiting their value as controlled evidence.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: the framework closely builds on Bottleneck Sampling-style resolution staging, correlated-noise treatment adapted from Pyramidal Flow Matching, and a simple Canny/top-k heuristic. The combination may be useful, but the limited ablation and reproducibility details prevent the manuscript from demonstrating that its specific novel elements account for the gains. strengths: RALU addresses a practically important and comparatively underexplored direction: training-free spatial acceleration of diffusion transformers. The combination of low-resolution denoising, selective early upsampling of edge regions, and final full-resolution refinement is intuitive and potentially useful.

The noise-timestep distribution-matching component is technically motivated. The paper derives the correlated-noise adjustment, states the positive-semidefinite constraint on its covariance, and formulates schedule selection as Jensen-Shannon divergence minimization rather than relying only on a heuristic schedule.

The empirical results are encouraging across two substantial flow-matching models. At approximately 7x acceleration on FLUX, RALU substantially improves over equal-cost Bottleneck Sampling in FID (28.68 versus 38.16), NIQE (6.87 versus 8.71), and CLIP-IQA (0.681 versus 0.631), while retaining comparable or better alignment. Similar gains appear on SD3 at approximately 2x and 3x acceleration.

The evaluation covers complementary aspects of generation: reference-based and no-reference image-quality metrics, two text-alignment benchmarks, latency, FLOPs, qualitative comparisons, and 192 stated uncurated FLUX samples. The preservation of quality is therefore supported by more than a few selected visual examples.

The method is training-free and complementary to temporal caching. The caching experiment provides concrete evidence of this compatibility, increasing FLUX speedups from 4.13x to 5.00x and from 7.02x to 7.94x with relatively modest metric changes. The manuscript is generally clear, visually effective, and candid about its restriction to flow-matching text-to-image models.
weaknesses: The principal material weakness is incomplete experimental specification. Although sample counts are given for GenEval and T2I-CompBench, the manuscript does not identify the prompt set, real-image reference distribution, or number of samples used for FID, NIQE, and CLIP-IQA. Latency reporting also omits batch size, precision, warm-up/repetition protocol, and variability. These omissions make the headline quality and speed comparisons difficult to reproduce precisely.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed components. There is no quantitative comparison of edge-selective early upsampling against random-region selection, uniform early upsampling at matched FLOPs, or a version without early upsampling. Likewise, the benefit of NT-DM over no rescheduling and over the baseline heuristic is shown mainly through a qualitative diagram rather than a comprehensive metric table.

Table 4 provides only small parameter perturbations around the selected NT-DM configuration and does not report the corresponding JSD values. Its evidence is mixed: the nominal configuration has the best NIQE, but other settings have better CLIP-IQA or GenEval. Thus, the claimed link between minimizing timestep-distribution divergence and maximizing generation quality is not strongly established.

Implementation details for mixed-resolution processing remain insufficient. The paper does not fully specify how high- and low-resolution tokens are packed, positionally encoded, masked, and mapped through each DiT block, nor how correlated noise with covariance I-cΣ is sampled efficiently. Stage schedules are supplied, but the absence of pseudocode or a stated code release limits reproducibility.

The theoretical presentation contains a notation inconsistency: Eq. (5)/Eq. (S2) labels the desired variable as an upsampled low-resolution latent while assigning it an isotropic high-resolution covariance. The intended target distribution can be inferred from the derivation, but it should be stated consistently. There are also minor presentation errors, including the incorrect downward arrow for GenEval in Table 4 and several grammatical or citation-model-name mistakes; these are refinements rather than reasons for rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important and comparatively underexplored direction: training-free spatial acceleration of diffusion transformers. The combination of region-adaptive mixed-resolution processing and noise/timestep matching is technically interesting and reasonably distinct from temporal caching and prior high-low-high sampling approaches.

The empirical results are broad and generally convincing. Evaluation covers two major flow-matching DiTs, several acceleration levels, five complementary quality/alignment metrics, FLOPs, latency on two GPU architectures, and memory. At comparable compute, RALU consistently improves over Bottleneck Sampling and usually over temporal baselines; for example, at roughly 7x FLUX acceleration it obtains ImageReward 0.999 versus 0.792 for Bottleneck Sampling and 0.920 for simply using seven steps.

The component analyses support the main design choices. The paper studies upsampling time, edge-region ratio, edge-detection strategy, upsampling operator, timestep-distribution divergence, and compatibility with temporal acceleration and distilled models. The qualitative comparisons and uncurated FLUX samples further support the claim that RALU reduces conspicuous boundary artifacts.

The covariance-matching argument provides useful motivation beyond a purely empirical recipe. For 2x nearest-neighbor upsampling, the paper derives a feasible corrective-noise covariance and corresponding scaling/timestep parameters, including the positive-semidefinite constraint on the correlation parameter.

The method is training-free and does not increase reported peak memory relative to the underlying models, making the contribution potentially useful in practice. The manuscript also clearly acknowledges that NT-Matching is currently restricted to flow-matching architectures.
weaknesses: The strongest wording is not fully supported by the numbers. Quality degradation is not always "negligible": at 3x acceleration on SD3, ImageReward falls from 0.971 to 0.798 and GenEval from 0.703 to 0.599. Likewise, the headline 15.91x result is measured relative to FLUX.1-dev, whereas RALU adds only about 1.34x over the already distilled FLUX.1-schnell baseline (11.83x to 15.91x). These are framing issues rather than failures of the underlying method, but the claims should be interpreted accordingly.

The theoretical treatment rests on an idealized conditional Gaussian flow trajectory and does not quantify how well actual pretrained-model states satisfy that assumption. Timestep matching is partly heuristic: the target mixture weights overlapping intervals by their raw lengths, despite the nonuniform base density, and the paper does not justify this choice against alternatives based on scheduler probability mass. The numerical-search ranges, discretization, and optimization procedure for the JSD objective are also unspecified.

There is a covariance inconsistency in the supplementary derivation. Equation S2 writes the next-stage target covariance as proportional to Sigma, while Equation S4 and the main-paper Equation 6 match to the identity covariance. The subsequent derivation appears to use the identity target, so this is likely a correctable equation error, but it should be fixed because it occurs in the central technical argument.

The artifact-ratio evidence is insufficiently documented. The paper does not state who or what labels an image as containing an artifact, provide annotation criteria or inter-rater agreement, or clearly give the sample count and uncertainty for Figure 7. Since "artifact-free" is a central claim, a blinded human evaluation or a fully specified reproducible detector would materially strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive supplement. Critical mechanics of constructing mixed-resolution token sequences, assigning positional coordinates/embeddings, merging early- and late-upsampled regions, sampling the negatively correlated corrective noise, and handling region boundaries are not described at implementation-level precision. No code or pseudocode is provided, and latency methodology lacks details such as warm-up, repetition count, variance, and whether text encoding is included.

The quantitative tables report only point estimates. Even with 5,000 COCO generations for several metrics, paired confidence intervals or significance tests are needed to interpret small differences such as T2I-CompBench changes of 0.001-0.01. Baseline hyperparameters also appear hand-selected without a documented common tuning protocol, leaving some uncertainty about fairness.

Generality is limited to two flow-matching text-to-image DiTs at one output resolution. This limitation does not negate the contribution, but evidence is absent for diffusion U-Nets, conventional diffusion parameterizations, other resolutions, or other modalities, so broader claims about DiTs or latent upsampling should remain qualified.

strengths: The manuscript presents a useful training-free spatial-acceleration direction for diffusion transformers, combining edge-selective mixed-resolution tokens with noise/timestep correction. The principal efficiency results are promising: RALU reaches 426 TFLOPs and 3.75 s on FLUX, versus 2991 TFLOPs and 25.1 s for the 50-step reference, while retaining substantially better automatic quality scores than similarly accelerated alternatives. On SD3, it likewise compares favorably at approximately 2x and 3x acceleration.

Evaluation covers two major flow-matching DiTs, several temporal and spatial baselines, measured latency on A100 and A6000 GPUs, FLOPs, memory, multiple quality/alignment benchmarks, and compatibility with temporal acceleration and distilled models.

The supplement supplies baseline configurations, scheduler parameters, hardware measurements, comparisons of edge detectors and upsamplers, and uncurated qualitative samples. These additions improve transparency.
The method's limitations are stated appropriately: NT-Matching is specialized to flow-matching models, and applicability beyond DiTs is not demonstrated.
weaknesses: Material: The evidence for the central artifact-mitigation claim is inadequate. Artifact ratio is never given an annotation definition, labeling protocol, annotator count, agreement statistic, or uncertainty. Figures 2, 3, and 7 therefore rely on an opaque subjective measurement. Canny edge energy is not an artifact-specific metric, and no human preference study validates the claimed perceptual advantage.

Material: Component isolation is weak. There is no quantitative, compute-matched ablation of naive upsampling, early regional upsampling alone, noise injection alone, timestep matching alone, and the full method. Figure 5 contains only one selected example, while Table 3 merely perturbs JSD around the chosen solution and lacks a no-matching baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not firmly establish which proposed component causes the reported gains.

Material: The mathematical account contains an internal contradiction. Main-paper Eq. 6 and supplementary Eq. S4 use an isotropic target covariance proportional to I, whereas Eq. S2 states that the next-stage covariance is proportional to Sigma. The subsequent derivation silently follows the former. Moreover, matching the distribution around Up(x1) does not establish equivalence to the true high-resolution clean-latent trajectory, so the claim of returning to the 'original trajectory' is stronger than the derivation supports.

Material: NT-Matching remains insufficiently reproducible. The paper says c and the stage shifts are determined 'analytically,' but Eq. S12 specifies numerical JSD minimization without its search domain, discretization, optimizer, or tie-breaking procedure. It also does not explain concretely how samples with covariance I-cSigma are generated, or fully specify construction and positional encoding of the mixed-resolution token sequence.

Material: Statistical support is missing. Reported benchmark scores have no variance, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests, even where differences are small. The claimed p<0.001 relationship in Section 3.2 lacks the test definition and underlying observations. The automatic metrics also cannot by themselves substantiate 'artifact-free' or 'negligible quality degradation.'

The strongest wording is overstated. At FLUX 7x, ImageReward falls from 1.095 to 0.999; adding RALU to FLUX-schnell reduces several scores, including GenEval from 0.688 to 0.636; and adding it to SD3.5L-Turbo reduces GenEval from 0.744 to 0.696. These may be acceptable efficiency tradeoffs, but they are not uniformly negligible.

Evaluation breadth is limited to 1024x1024 text-to-image generation on two closely related flow-matching DiTs. There is no resolution scaling analysis, robustness analysis across prompt or image complexity, or comparison on non-flow diffusion architectures. This limits the demonstrated generality but is not independently rejection-determining.

Presentation: Several details should be corrected or clarified, including the covariance inconsistency, the unexplained artifact labeling, and whether qualitative comparisons use identical prompts and initial seeds. Overall, the promising empirical contribution is near the acceptance boundary, but the missing component-level and perceptual validation prevents a confident acceptance recommendation.

strengths: RALU addresses a practically important and comparatively underexplored direction: training-free spatial acceleration of diffusion transformers. The combination of low-resolution sampling, selective early upsampling of edge regions, and noise/timestep matching is technically motivated and more substantive than simply changing the sampling resolution.

The empirical results are strong across two major flow-matching text-to-image models. At comparable compute, RALU consistently outperforms Bottleneck Sampling and most temporal baselines; the gains are especially convincing at aggressive settings such as FLUX at approximately 7× speedup and SD3 at approximately 3× speedup.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: 5,000 COCO generations are used for several quality metrics, compositional alignment is tested with GenEval and T2I-CompBench, and the paper reports FLOPs, latency on A100 and A6000 GPUs, and memory usage. The extensive qualitative and uncurated results support the claim that obvious artifacts are substantially reduced.

The ablations examine the early-upsampling ratio, NT-Matching, edge detection in image versus latent space, fixed versus adaptive region selection, and alternative interpolation methods. These experiments generally support the main design choices.

Compatibility with temporal acceleration and timestep-distilled models is useful in practice. The demonstrated combinations reach up to 9.03× training-free acceleration and 15.91× relative speedup with a distilled model, showing that the spatial approach is complementary rather than a competing replacement.
The manuscript is well organized, clearly motivates the acceleration/artifact trade-off, and provides detailed baseline configurations and stage schedules in the appendix.
weaknesses: The mathematical presentation of NT-Matching contains a consequential inconsistency. Main-text Eq. (6) specifies an isotropic target covariance proportional to I, whereas supplementary Eq. (S2) states a covariance proportional to Σ; the following Eq. (S4) again uses I. Because covariance correction is the central technical argument, the intended target and derivation should be stated consistently.

The mixed-resolution computation is underspecified. The paper does not give an algorithm or sufficiently precise account of how high- and low-resolution tokens are jointly represented, indexed, masked, assigned positional embeddings, and passed through each DiT block. Likewise, implementation of sampling from the structured covariance I-cΣ is not described. These omissions hinder independent reproduction.

The central artifact-ratio experiments lack an annotation protocol. The manuscript does not define operational criteria for an artifact, state who labeled the images, report agreement or uncertainty, or explain whether assessment was blinded. Consequently, claims such as “artifact-free” and the large advantage in Fig. 7 are less well supported than the automatic-metric results.

The claim of negligible quality degradation is too broad. Relative to the full models, text-alignment degradation is noticeable in several settings: for example, FLUX GenEval falls from 0.698 to 0.652 at the reported 5.53× setting, and SD3 GenEval falls from 0.703 to 0.599 at 3.02×. The distilled-model combinations also show nontrivial metric losses.

The evidence relies almost entirely on automatic metrics and selected qualitative comparisons; no controlled human preference study is provided. This matters because the claimed benefit specifically concerns perceptual aliasing and mismatching artifacts, for which ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, and NIQE are imperfect proxies.

Generality is demonstrated only on two closely related flow-matching text-to-image DiTs at 1024×1024 resolution. Applicability to other diffusion parameterizations, resolutions, architectures, or modalities remains unverified, and the optimized schedules are model-and-speedup specific.

The NT-Matching ablation varies JSD only over a narrow range and changes parameters jointly, so it establishes correlation rather than isolating whether timestep-distribution matching itself causes the improvements. Statistical uncertainty is also absent for most reported quality metrics.
